analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $6.50 an hour.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage to $6.50 was sent to a House committee and its subcommittee, never got a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed the federal wage floor from $4.25 an hour to $6.50 an hour, starting 90 days after it became law [S2][S3]. It applied to employers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act, the law that sets the federal minimum wage [S2][S3]. It was introduced in January 1995, referred to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities, then sent to its Subcommittee on Workforce Protections — and no further action was ever taken [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning between $4.25 and $6.50 an hour would see their pay rise — the largest group being workers in restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service jobs. Their households and communities would also benefit as wages rose.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $6.50 an hour, effective 90 days after enactment [S2][S3].
Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, the law covering the federal wage floor for most hourly workers [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay wages between the old and new floors — concentrated in restaurants, fast food, retail, and other service businesses — would bear higher payroll costs, and economists debate how much of that cost is passed to consumers through prices or absorbed through reduced hiring or hours.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers like restaurants and retail

drawbacks.text: A 53% increase in the wage floor — from $4.25 to $6.50 — is a large jump, and employers paying near the old minimum would face materially higher labor costs [S2][S3].
The bill contains no phase-in schedule beyond the initial 90 days, no small-business exemption, and no tip-credit adjustment, so the full increase lands at once on covered employers [S3].

Opponents of minimum wage increases argue they can reduce hours or entry-level hiring for the least experienced workers; supporters counter that decades of research find modest effects at moderate increases, though a jump of this size is above what most studies tested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A direct, simple raise for workers at the bottom of the pay scale — the group with the least bargaining power. The cost falls on the employers of those workers and, in part, on consumers through prices. The main design weakness is the abruptness: a single 90-day jump to $6.50 with no phase-in gives employers little adjustment time, which a more gradual schedule would have softened.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House committee and then a subcommittee, and never moved again — no hearing, no vote, nothing — until the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Martin Olav Sabo introduced the Minimum Wage Amendments of 1995 on January 20, 1995 [S1][S5].
The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $6.50 an hour [S2][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities on January 20, 1995, and to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on February 1, 1995 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].
It drew 22 cosponsors — 21 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay near the minimum wage — concentrated in restaurants, retail, and other service industries — kept the lower $4.25 wage floor, and low-wage workers never received the raise. The House majority that controlled the committee agenda avoided a vote on the issue.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent — no Republican supported the bill — and the Republican-controlled committee and House majority took no action on it.

industries.note: Restaurants are the largest employer of minimum-wage workers, so a $6.50 floor would raise their labor costs directly. The industry's interest in keeping the wage at $4.25 ran directly against the pay of the workers it employs.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Retailers and service businesses paying between $4.25 and $6.50 would face higher payroll costs, with some of the cost likely passed to customers in prices.
